region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 38

summary.en: A bragging mother offers her daughter to the best singer, dancer, archer, and best-dressed suitor in turn, and the girl laughs them all off — until the Wasp's glittering blue kaross wins her. He feeds her on spiders and grubs; when she mocks his thin body, he shoots her dead on the spot. So the mother got the payment for all her parading.
summary.zh: 誇口之母輪流以「最善歌者」「最善舞者」「最善射者」「最美衣者」許嫁其女，女皆笑而拒之——直至馬蜂之閃爍藍裘得之。他以蛛與蛹飼妻；妻譏其瘦軀，他即射殺之。母之炫燿，報應如此。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; contains domestic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 38 (1920); not verbatim. The mother's greatest amusement was to praise her children in their faces before others... she offered the girl to the one who could sing the most beautifully. Cricket came singing, Sunbeetle came singing, Owl came singing, Wolf and Jackal came singing; but the girl, to the great consternation of the mother, burst out laughing and mocked the singers to their faces.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 38; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Another time she offered the girl to the one who danced the most finely: Frog danced, Springbok, Hare, Snake, Partridge, Tortoise — and again the girl sat and laughed the whole lot of dancers in their faces. Then again: the one who could shoot the neatest with an arrow should have her; and Honeybee shot, Mosquito shot, Gnat, Blindfly and Flea shot — and the company scattered with smarting eyes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 38; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Then the mother said the one with the most beautiful kaross could have her daughter: Moth came with his, Mouse, Lizard, Sugarbird, Zebra, Mongoose — and Wasp with his; and they opened their karosses to show how beautiful they were — only Wasp did not. The girl promised solemnly not to laugh, and her choice fell on the glittering blue kaross of Wasp; they went together to his clay house with its many chambers. But he caught only caterpillars, worms and spiders; when she saw his thin body and laughed 'so that is why you never took your kaross off!', he shot her dead on the spot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 38; not verbatim.

title.en: Mother Lion and the Stolen Children

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 39

summary.en: The old lions catch Bushman children alive at the water-pool; a decoy 'woman' dancing under a tree lures father Lion to his death by poisoned arrows. Mother Lion raises the stolen children, feeding them a forgetful fruit, hunting with them in the night; a brave Bushman feeds them charm-wood, and each remembers: 'Your parents' fire burns under that krans — see the smoke!' She weeps her grey age; the parents spring out of their skins for joy.
summary.zh: 老獅於池邊活捕桑童；假「婦人」於樹下起舞誘雄獅至，毒箭斃之。母獅養被擄之童，飼以忘憂之果，夜率其獵。勇桑人以巫木飼之，眾童記憶復甦：「爾父母之火燃於彼崖下——見煙乎！」。母獅泣其灰老；父母見子復歡騰。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 39 (1920); not verbatim. The old Father Lion and Mother Lion grew old and toothless; they could no longer hunt well, and began to catch among the Bushmen — especially the old maids who went to seek veld-food — and to catch the children alive and carry them home to live and play under their trees by the great rocks. The Bushmen made an old pop of skins and stuffed it with grass so that it looked at a distance like a real Bushman; two hunters climbed a tree and pulled the string so the pop danced.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 39; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Father Lion thought it was an old maid who could not climb a tree; he stalked the pop, the hunters made a noise above, and as he opened his mouth wide they shot poisoned arrows straight into it, and after a few moments Father Lion was a carcass, never again to catch old maids and children. Mother Lion had watched the murder of her old man all the time; she armed the Bushman children she kept with knobkerries and went with them by night to hunt.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 39; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. By her house grew a great dark-green tree with delicious fruit: as soon as the children ate of it they forgot everything that had happened before, so that they quite forgot they had Bushmen for parents... One day a brave Bushman heard the children playing and laughing under Mother Lion's tree. He had 'houtjies' in his knapsack — wood-chips his sorcery-doctor had given him — and let all the children chew of it, and their former understanding came back.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 39; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. 'You two that sit there, your parents' fire burns under that krans; do you see the smoke shooting out there?' And the two children sprang up and ran home to their parents' house; and so, child by child, all ran off. Mother Lion came back with the water, out of breath, and wept bitterly: 'You have taken the children from here. They were so contented here... Can you not see I am growing grey and old?'... And the parents of the children wanted to spring out of their skins for joy when they saw their children again playing round them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 39; not verbatim.

title.en: The Lion in the Hut by the Child

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 41

summary.en: A girl who cries all night for Bushman-rice brings the lion into the hut's doorway; while the parents lie rigid under their skins, the child tickles the lion with a stick — 'Ek 'tieke jou!' — and at last stuffs a burning brand into his long mane. The lion bolts with the veld aflame behind him and drops dead; and the parents give the child a whole eggshell of Bushman-rice, for she saved them from death.
summary.zh: 夜哭索蟻卵飯之女引獅入屋門；父母僵臥皮褥之下，孩童以小枝撓獅——「我騷你！」——終以燃柴塞入其長鬣。獅火焚原野而逃，終倒斃；父母酬以滿蛋殼之蟻卵飯，因其救全家於死。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 41 (1920); not verbatim. A Bushman and his wife had only one girl child who had just begun to talk... they dug Bushman-rice, shot a springbok on the way home, roasted and boiled and ate straight through; and late in the night they went to sleep under their skins — but the child not: she sat crying at the fire for Bushman-rice, and would not stop, till she began to cry loudly.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 41; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Lion heard the child and came creeping; he saw the child alone by the fire while the parents lay under their skins... Lion came and sat in the doorway of the big hut; now nobody could flee. He meant to eat the parents and not the child, so he began sedately to play with the child: he put out his paw, took hold of her and played like a cat with her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 41; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The parents wanted to die of anguish, but scarcely drew breath; yet the child found this play of Lion's very fine; she laughed at it and said every time: 'Ek 'tieke jou! Ek 'tieke jou!' while she tickled and pricked Lion with a little stick. At last the child gripped a burning brand with a little flame from under the pot and stuffed the flame into the long mane-hair of Lion; the hair caught fire, and the more Lion shook his head the more the flames roared. He took to his heels, and as far as he ran he set the veld alight; then the parents first looked out from under the skins... they saw the veld burn, Lion running about in full flame, and at last drop dead to the ground.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 41; not verbatim.

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 42

summary.en: The gluttonous Wolf eats his neighbours bare and is burnt out of three bush-houses; he lodges in holes, woos a girl for his second wife, and to fetch her necklace from a rock-slit enlists the dung-beetle — 'you roll your ball backwards because you can see the whole world round about you' — to hook it out with its horn. He wins the girl and two wives, and the neighbours' proverb is born: 'Give him two wives.'
summary.zh: 饞狼食盡鄰人、三度茅屋被焚；匿居穴中，另聘一女為二房；取岩縫中之項鍊時求助於糞金龜——「汝倒推糞球，因可環顧四周」——以角鉤出項鍊。既得二妻，鄰人諺語遂生：「予其二妻。」

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 42 (1920); not verbatim. Wolf was, and is to this day, a quick hunter; but he eats a great deal, and it takes a big knapsack of meat to silence his hunger... When the neighbours heard him coming they hid the food away; but his scent is good, and he begged and insisted so shamelessly that at last they gave him something to eat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 42; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. At last they set fire to his bush-houses — one after another — till he moved quite to another place, and lived in holes, for ground- and rock-houses cannot be set alight. Wolf and his wife each went their own way so far that they never came to the same place... One evening he went courting and saw a young girl after his own heart, and told his tales of hunting and strength; three evenings later she said: 'Go and seek my necklace and bring it here, then I shall take you.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 42; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He lay downwind and heard where she had hidden it: in the rock-slit by the 'norra-karee tree, in the ear of a kudu. He hooked with a stick but the mice had eaten the ear's underpoint, and the necklace slipped deeper than he could reach. Then came Mistkruiwer (the dung-beetle) rolling a ball of clay backwards; Wolf mocked him as a fool, and the beetle answered: 'I am not so stupid: if I push the ball behind-foremost I can see the whole world round about me... I am strong and can push far bigger pieces of clay than this!' Wolf wagered him the necklace; the beetle stepped into the slit, hooked it out with its horn, and threw it down before Wolf. So Wolf got his second wife — and the neighbours said the best punishment was: 'Give him two wives.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 42; not verbatim.

title.en: The Leopard Is Displeased with the Sun

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 43

summary.en: The leopard, of the old race and a hater of the new Sun's heat, scolds all day, is ringed by his own burning veld, and leaps blind through the flames that singe his coat bonter. He dens in a cool cave, kills an old hartebeest in drizzle, and — pretending to be a weary traveller — creeps into the Bushmen's thorn-kraal by night; the sharp-eyed maid sees his feet, lures the family out with a tale of ostrich eggs, and the archers shoot him through the chinks.
summary.zh: 豹本古族，恨新日之炎，終日咒罵；野火自焚其境，閉目躍過烈焰，毛色愈斑。遂居涼穴；細雨中殺老公羚；夜間佯為倦旅混入桑人之荊欄。利眼侍女見其足，以「鴕蛋」謊語誘全家出，弓手自隙射之，豹斃於欄中。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; graphic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 43 (1920); not verbatim. The Leopard built his house there on the plain among tall grass and bushes. He is also one of the old race, who walked about when there was as yet no Sun; therefore he is Leopard. He was only angry at the children who threw the Sun's head into the sky to make it so bright by day and cause such unbearable heat; therefore he never had a good word for the Sun, but scolded the Sun the whole day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 43; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. One day it was very hot; the Sun set the veld ablaze with his great heat, and when the Leopard smelt the fire and heard it crackle he sprang out, ringed on all sides by flames; there was nothing else for it but to shut his eyes and leap straight through the roaring flames — that singed and burnt the hair of his spotted kaross so that it became only the more spotted. He found a beautiful koppie with a rock cave shaded by great trees and took up his dwelling there, for 'the Sun cannot shoot his warm arrows through the great rocks.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 43; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. In drizzle he caught an old hartebeest, and while he lay on an overhanging branch the Jackal's begging betrayed him. When he came back the Bushmen had hedged the hartebeest in with a thorn-kraal, waiting for him. So he wrapped himself tight in his kaross, walked up and said he was a traveller who wanted only a sleeping-place, no food, and had a heavy headache — and sat in a dark corner. A maid's stone-knife slipped and fell near his feet; as she sought it she saw the Leopard's two feet sticking out under the kaross. Without a sound she cried: 'We are roasting meat here and forgetting a nest full of ostrich eggs! Come, it is dark; let us all go and fetch the eggs' — and she winked her husband out with the family. Then the three men drew their bows and shot at the Leopard through the branches; he could not flee, for the little gate was shut behind them — and so the Leopard met his end inside the kraal.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 43; not verbatim.

title.en: Porcupine and Bat: The Orphans' Night-Sight
title.zh: 豪豬與蝙蝠：孤兒之夜眼

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 44

summary.en: A cruel stepmother starves her stepchildren; the dead mother sends the Owl, who plays father, leads them to his cliff, changes the boy into a porcupine — his arrows become quills in his kaross — and the girl into a bat, giving them fireflies so they can see by night. Their mother becomes a second owl that visits them; and the porcupine's sleep-charm quills can be dodged by the knowing.
summary.zh: 惡繼母餓其繼子；亡母遣梟假扮父親，引二子至崖居，化子為豪豬——其箭化為裘上之刺——化女為蝙蝠，並賜螢火使其夜能視。亡母化為另一梟夜夜探望；豪豬之催眠刺，知情者可避。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 44 (1920); not verbatim. In the old days there was an old Bushman and his old wife who belonged to the old race, and they had a little boy and a little girl as their only children. When the mother died the girl was still very young; now they were orphans. The father took another wife — a young woman who did not care for other people's children, and her two stepchildren did not have it good under her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 44; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. For the little boy she deliberately had springbok skins laid out to play on, and smeared the bow his father had made for him with springbok fat, so that the spirit of the springboks drew into the boy and his bow, and all the springboks in the veld feared him and never gave him a chance to come near... For the little girl the stepmother neglected everything, and the poor child lived mostly on little insects and flies.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 44; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. One evening the dead mother of the two children sent the Owl to them. The Owl is a sorcerer and can change himself into a man or an owl; and he played himself before them as their own father. He took them to the rock kranses where he lived, gave them veld-food and veld-fruit, changed the boy into a Porcupine — his arrows, of which there were many, he changed into quills that stuck fast in the kaross of the boy, so that nobody dared touch him — and the girl he changed into a Bat, which lives on insects to this day; and he gave them fireflies to eat, so that they could see well in the dark. From then on they can only see by night and are blind in the day when the sun shines.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 44; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Their mother, changed into another kind of owl, visits them by night; the porcupine knows all the tricks of porcupine-hunters, whose eyelids grow heavy under his sleeping-charm, and when he is found first he shoots his quills and is off — but the Bushmen know all his tricks.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 44; not verbatim.

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 45

summary.en: A maid who has eaten a jackal's heart dreams a lion is biting her and wakes the whole camp; her dream is laughed off. Next morning the tickling behind her man's back means gemsbok blood; the children spy the herd, the hunters creep out — and one finds himself a stone's throw from a lion stalking the same gemsbok. He climbs, shoots, and kills gemsbok and lion with one arrow.
summary.zh: 食豺心之侍女夢獅噬己，驚醒全營；其夢遭眾人訕笑。翌晨其夫背後之癢意味大羚之血；孩童窺得羚群，獵者潛出——其中一人發現自己與伺羚之獅近在咫尺。他攀樹射之，一箭連斃羚與獅。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; graphic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 45 (1920); not verbatim. One of the maids had set the liver and heart of the jackal for herself in a little pot on the fire, for the children may not eat of this — especially not the heart. A jackal is very timid, and if children eat its heart they grow up as cowards and bolt at the smallest rustle; therefore the Bushmen never give the jackal's heart to their children.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 45; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When all was quiet and everyone snored aloud, the maid had a ghastly dream, and she began to scream as if she were being murdered: 'Here is a lion! He is biting me! Help, help!' The men searched with bows and assegais and found nothing, and her husband laughed: 'O, I know what it is: it is the heart of the jackal that now comes to frighten you!' — 'Dreams lie!' — 'Wait, you shall see that this dream that came to warn me is not for nothing.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 45; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Next morning over the meat her husband sat suddenly still and said: 'I feel my flesh creep on my back; that means a gemsbok is scratching its back with its horn near here... it means we shall shoot gemsbok and carry them home, for it is their blood that runs down behind my back.' He sent the children to climb the koppie and look; the children whispered back: gemsbok lay just below. The hunters crept out, and the man who had felt the creeping hid behind a thick tree-stem — and saw, a little before him, a giant of a lion also stalking the gemsbok. He climbed, shot as the lion seized the buck, and the arrow struck the lion in the flank; so the tree-climber got a gemsbok and a lion with one arrow-shot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 45; not verbatim.

title.en: The Hammerkop and the Swallows: Children of the Moon

region.zh: 南非德蘭士瓦（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; told by a Transvaal Bushman in 1885 to G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 46

summary.en: Swallows are the children of the Sun: murdered Bushman children who lie dead in the hollow moon until it waxes, then drop from the sky as swallows and build their crescent nests under the krans. The Hammerkop warns of a Kaffir raiding party; the first kraal that stoned the birds is massacred, the second, warned by the old wise man, shoots the raiders from the rocks. The black raiders become the mieland-raiding crows.
summary.zh: 燕為日之子：被殺之桑童屍月之空匙，月盈則自天墜為燕，於崖下築半月之巢。鎚頭鸛預警科薩劫掠隊；第一村擲石驅鳥者遭屠，第二村中老智者得警，據石射殺掠者。黑掠者化為劫米田之烏鴉。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; colonial-era interethnic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 46 (1920); not verbatim. The swallows (krans-swallows) make their little houses under the overhanging rock; their nests look like the moon with its two horns standing up... for the Hammerkop told them to build them so. Now, the moon, when it makes a bowl upward, carries the bodies of people who have only just died; and the swallows are dead little children come alive again. When the moon becomes half again the hollow vanishes, and then there is no more place for the children; so they fall out of the sky and become swallows.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 46; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. One evening the Hammerkop saw in the water that a great murdering band of long black people was on the march. He flew out at once and called the Owl, and the two flew to warn the Bushmen. At the first kraal they were clapped at and stoned and flew away grieved; at the second kraal an ancient Bushman, who was wise, bade the others be still and listen: 'the two birds come to warn us that a murdering band is coming and the little kraal's folk must be ready.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 46; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. That evening many little stars shot; the swallows feared the fire-lights; but the Hammerkop looked and saw: 'Now the great black ones are murdering out the little brown ones... at the first kraal, where the Owl and I were yesterday; they there would not believe us.' Later in the night more stars with long tails shot: 'Be at rest; the great black ones are now attacking at the second kraal, where the Bushmen sit armed in a stone hedge and shoot the great black ones dead in heaps — I can see in the water how they roll over.'... When the Moon's hollow had grown level again the bodies dropped from the Moon, and the Sun sent the brown children of the Bushmen alive to the Hammerkop: they became swallows. And the great black ones the Sun changed into black crows, which make such a noise as the raiders did; and so the black folk departed and plague the mielie-lands to this day, while the Hammerkop and the Sun's children, the swallows, dwell together in love in the kranses.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 46; not verbatim.

title.en: The Clouds: Hair, Feathers and the Whirlwind That Carries the Dead

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 47

summary.en: The storm-wind is the breath of the Great Bird that dwells in a mountain hole. A dead person's hair becomes clouds; the whirlwind lifts the corpse — even buried — and lays it gently in the bowl between the horns of the new moon; the mist-cloud covers the rising dead so none see them; and the rocks, which cursed wind and cloud, can never wake again.
summary.zh: 暴風乃居山穴之大鳥之氣息。死者之髮化為雲；旋風捲屍（縱已葬）輕置於新月雙角之空匙；霧雲掩護復起之死者使其不見；詛咒風雲之岩石則永不復醒。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 47 (1920); not verbatim. All the clouds are not of one kind: there are clouds that pour out rain, and others that are dry; there are thunder-clouds that hold water, fire and thunder-stones; and there are those that hold only hair, feathers and wind. The wind is the breath of everything that lives; so the storm-winds are the breath of the Great Bird, which lives in a hole in the mountains, can hide itself in clouds, and flies to the sea to fetch rain.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 47; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When a person dies his hair becomes clouds; when a bird dies its feathers also become clouds. But such clouds give no rain, for they are only hair and feathers without water; they come and vanish without letting fall a drop. If a person has died, his footprints still stand fresh in the sand as if he lived; therefore the storm-wind comes and blows the footprints of the dead level with the sand.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 47; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When a corpse lies dead on the earth, the wind makes a strong whirlwind; and it takes the corpse up — even though buried under the ground — and carries it to the hollow bowl between the two standing horns of the new moon, and lays it gently therein. Therefore the Bushmen bury a corpse in a sitting posture: it must at any time be ready to stand up. Before Death came into the world through the Hare, people and animals slept only till new moon, and then came alive again like the moon; but now they must sit long in their graves before they will one day come alive again. Then the person's cloud comes down and drifts like a heavy mist over the grave to cover the rising one, so that the others cannot see that the dead has come alive again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 47; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The rocks also were first Bushmen of the old race; they cursed the wind and the clouds when the storms blinded them while they stalked springbok, so that they shot all their arrows in vain and tore the skins of their thumbs with the great strain of the bowstrings. The wind and the clouds sent a Kaffir band upon them, and the mist and dust hid the Bushmen so completely that the raiders killed them all without risk; the scattered corpses of the dead Bushmen turned to stone. Therefore the wind and the clouds resolved never again to raise the rocks: now they are struck, trampled and kicked by all who pass.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 47; not verbatim.

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 48

summary.en: In drought two Bushman families follow the game; the old man calls the Great Water-Snake with buchu and praise, and at morning finds a never-dry pool where jackals drink — he shoots the jackal family for meat. Then, faithless, they steal the Snake's shining stone; the snake has the lions track and kill the sleepers, spares the children in the cracks, and the orphaned little ones become the meerkats and the ground-squirrels that live together in the same holes.
summary.zh: 旱時兩桑人家庭隨獸遷徙；老人以布庫草與讚辭召大水蛇，晨至不涸之池，射殺飲水之豺一家為食。繼而背信，竊蛇之閃石；蛇令獅循跡殺其眠者，赦石縫中之童；孤兒遂化為狐獴與地松鼠，至今同穴而居。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; graphic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 48 (1920); not verbatim. There was a drought that grew ever harder; the waters gave out, and the game moved away; so Bushmen and animals too had to follow — all in the track of the game. Two house-families of Bushmen moved together... their children cried continually for food and water; and here and there they caught a tortoise or mice and lizards to keep their children alive.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 48; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. One evening, when the children were near dying of thirst, the old Bushman heard the Great Water-Snake crawling under the ground. He strewed pounded buchu on the ground so the snake could smell it, praised the snake, spoke fair to it, until the snake answered under the ground: 'In the morning light I shall have food and water for you Bushmen.' At daybreak the snake called: 'Go to those trees by the great rocks; on that flat rock-plate is a very deep pool of water that never goes dry... take your bows, you shall find something to shoot.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 48; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. By the water they found Jackal with his wife and children; he fled timidly, but the Bushmen shot his wife and all his children dead, drank, filled the eggshells, and roasted the jackal meat. Then faithless thoughts came to them: they spied out where the snake buried his shining stone, took it, and fled far away. The snake got the lions to follow the Bushmen's spoor; they bit the grown people dead, and the children fled into narrow cracks where the lions could not reach them. Then Jackal and Korhaan watched the children by day and night; the children whose karosses were of game-skins became meerkats, and those with karosses of young jackal skins became ground-squirrels — and they have always lived together in the same holes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 48; not verbatim.

title.en: The Tree That Dies Every Month on the Moon

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 49

summary.en: The rascal Tatsie, made witless by a tortoise heart slipped into his meat, is shot, drowned, suffocated — and revives each time. At last he wakes in the hollow of the new moon, brawls there, clings to a horn, breaks it off, and falls dead to earth. The broken horn grows into a monstrous fruit tree that ripens with each full moon and dies with it; and the Bushmen feast month after month in the land where the old race still lives.
summary.zh: 無賴塔茨西因肉中暗藏龜心而失智；被射、被溺、被窒息——皆復生。最後醒於新月之空匙，於月上鬧事，攀其角不捨，角折而墜地斃命。斷角長成參天果樹，隨月盈而熟、月落而枯；桑人月月赴宴——於古族猶存之地。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 49 (1920); not verbatim. Tatsie was a wonderful Bushman of the old race: he robbed, stole, murdered, and could conjure like few could imitate him... If a maid had cooked Bushman-rice he simply grabbed the pot before her and ate himself cudgel-full; if they scolded him he simply threw the rice into the fire and smashed the pot on top.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 49; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He let slip that if he ate the heart and liver of a tortoise he became for a time as witless as a tortoise; a crafty maid saved up the hearts and livers, and slipped one into the meat she chose out for him. When Tatsie's wits grew dim they shot him with a poisoned arrow; but the next morning Tatsie came walking along singing, knowing nothing of what had happened to him — he only told how deliciously he had slept and dreamed. They shot him with three arrows, sank him in a deep pool with a stone about his neck, and pressed a tortoise shell over his face till he died — and again he came walking along in the morning singing.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 49; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. But that evening the new moon had just shown itself in the west after sunset. In the night came a whirlwind, and it took the corpse away to the moon, to be laid between the horns in the hollow bowl. There Tatsie woke sober, and could not understand how he had got out to the moon; and there he fell to brawling with the other dead creatures, and they, sick of him, wanted to throw him out of the moon. He clung to one of the horns and held on; but the point of the horn broke off, and Tatsie came down with the piece of moon-horn in his hand, head downwards, and fell on the earth so that he hiccoughed. But he was dead, dead as a stone; never again would he come alive, for there was only a wet patch where he fell, and nothing more.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 49; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. But as the moon grew day after day, so the horn of the moon also began to grow into a tree, and grew greater day by day: flowers, leaves and fruits came on it, and it became a tremendous great tree spreading its branches far out on all sides. And when the moon was full, the tree was overloaded with many delicious fruits, which taste like meat and are as nourishing; the Bushmen came from all sides to eat of that delicious fruit. But after full moon the moon begins to die; this tree does the same: its fruits grew drier day by day and became like biltong, and when it was nearly new moon the tree — trunk and all — was dead to the ground. Then the Bushmen mourned; but when the new moon showed itself again the tree budded again, flowered and bore again, and the feasting went on month after month. There in the land where the old race still lives the tree stands to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 49; not verbatim.
